content: Propionic acid, also known systematically as propanoic acid, is a naturally occurring carboxylic acid with the chemical formula CH3CH2COOH. In its pure form, it is a colorless, corrosive liquid with a strong, pungent odor. The anion CH3CH2COO−, along with the salts and esters of propionic acid, are referred to as propionates or propanoates. Propionic acid was first identified in 1844 by Johann Gottlieb, who discovered it among the degradation products of sugar. Over the following years, other chemists synthesized propionic acid through various methods, unaware they were producing the same compound. In 1847, French chemist Jean-Baptiste Dumas confirmed that these acids were identical and named the compound propionic acid, derived from the Greek words protos (first) and pion (fat), as it was the smallest fatty acid to exhibit properties characteristic of other fatty acids, such as forming an oily layer when salted out of water and producing a soapy potassium salt. The physical properties of propionic acid are intermediate between those of smaller carboxylic acids, such as formic and acetic acids, and larger fatty acids. It is miscible with water but can be separated from water by adding salt. Its vapor deviates significantly from the ideal gas law due to the formation of hydrogen-bonded molecular pairs, a phenomenon also observed in its liquid state. Propionic acid shares the general chemical properties of carboxylic acids and can form derivatives such as amides, esters, anhydrides, and chlorides. It undergoes alpha-halogenation with bromine in the presence of phosphorus tribromide (PBr3) as a catalyst, producing CH3CHBrCOOH (via the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction). Industrially, propionic acid is primarily synthesized through the hydrocarboxylation of ethylene using nickel carbonyl as a catalyst. It can also be produced via the aerobic oxidation of propionaldehyde, a reaction that proceeds efficiently at mild temperatures (40–50°C) in the presence of cobalt or manganese ions. Historically, large quantities of propionic acid were generated as a byproduct of acetic acid production. Currently, BASF is the world's largest producer, with an annual production capacity of approximately 80 kilotons. Biologically, propionic acid is produced as its coenzyme A ester, propionyl-CoA, during the metabolic breakdown of odd-chain fatty acids and certain amino acids. Bacteria of the genus Propionibacterium produce propionic acid as a byproduct of anaerobic metabolism. These bacteria are commonly found in the stomachs of ruminants and human sweat glands, contributing to the characteristic odors of Swiss cheese and sweat. Propionic acid is widely used as a preservative due to its ability to inhibit the growth of mold and certain bacteria. It is commonly employed in animal feed, either directly or as its ammonium salt, and in human foods, particularly bread and baked goods, as its sodium or calcium salts. It is also used in older antifungal foot powders. Additionally, propionic acid serves as a chemical intermediate in the modification of synthetic cellulose fibers and the production of pesticides and pharmaceuticals. Its esters are occasionally used as solvents or artificial flavorings. The primary hazard associated with propionic acid is its potential to cause chemical burns upon contact with concentrated liquid. Long-term exposure to small amounts of propionic acid in laboratory animals has been associated with esophageal and stomach ulceration due to its corrosive nature. However, no toxic, mutagenic, carcinogenic, or reproductive effects have been observed. In the human body, propionic acid is readily metabolized and does not bioaccumulate. Recent research by MacFabe and colleagues demonstrated that intraventricular infusions of propionic acid in rats produced reversible behaviors resembling autism, including hyperactivity, dystonia, turning, and retropulsion. The treated rats also exhibited caudate spiking and the progressive development of limbic kindled seizures. The study concluded that this represents an excellent animal model of autism and warrants further investigation. The metabolism of propionic acid begins with its conversion to propionyl coenzyme A (propionyl-CoA), the typical first step in carboxylic acid metabolism. However, due to its three-carbon structure, propionyl-CoA cannot directly enter beta-oxidation or the citric acid cycle. In most vertebrates, propionyl-CoA is carboxylated to D-methylmalonyl-CoA, isomerized to L-methylmalonyl-CoA, and rearranged to form succinyl-CoA via a vitamin B12-dependent enzyme. Succinyl-CoA is an intermediate in the citric acid cycle and can be readily incorporated into it. In propionic acidemia, propionate acts as a metabolic toxin in liver cells by accumulating in mitochondria as propionyl-CoA and its derivative, methylcitrate, both of which inhibit the tricarboxylic acid cycle. Propionate is metabolized oxidatively by glial cells, suggesting astrocytic vulnerability in propionic acidemia when intramitochondrial propionyl-CoA accumulates. This condition may also alter neuronal and glial gene expression by affecting histone acetylation. Human skin hosts a bacterial species known as Propionibacterium acnes, named for its ability to produce propionic acid. This bacterium resides primarily in the sebaceous glands of the skin and is a principal cause of acne.
